```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(AKCatchments)
options(AKCatchments.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "ak_vignette_cache"))
```

The expected whole-rock content of nitrogen, sulfur and the major oxides
(SiO2, Al2O3, Fe2O3, CaO, MgO, Na2O, K2O, P2O5) under each catchment, as a
continuous exposure with its uncertainty. It joins two products:

- the **lithologies of each map unit** of the Geologic Map of Alaska
  (Wilson et al. 2015, USGS SIM 3340), with a rank saying how much of the
  unit each lithology makes up (`vignette("geology-sim3340")`);
- the **lithology geochemistry of Olson and Hawkins** (2014 data release,
  method in Olson and Hawkins 2012): a central value of each element for
  each lithology class, from EarthChem whole-rock analyses and the
  literature.

Olson and Hawkins built their CONUS rasters (the rock %N and oxide layers
behind StreamCat) the same way, from the CONUS state geologic map
databases. SIM 3340 comes from the same USGS integrated geologic map
database series, with the same lithology hierarchy and rank scheme, so
their method carries over map unit by map unit. To our knowledge it had not
been applied to Alaska: their products are built on NHDPlusV2, which
covers only the conterminous US.

Input, as for every layer: catchments (sf polygons with `site_code`, one
row per catchment, any CRS; a single `ak_delineate()` result, a list of
them, `ak_catchments()` output or your own polygons). Chunks that download
data are not run when this vignette is built; chunks that only compute
are. The other layers are listed in `vignette("delineation")`, section 7.

## 1. Getting the data

Automatic, once, into the cache:

- the SIM 3340 geodatabase (`ak_geology/`, shared with `ak_geology()`);
- two workbooks from the Olson and Hawkins data release
  (doi:10.5066/F7X0653P), into `olson_lithology/`:
  - **Lith-Nutrient**: N and S, 284 lithology classes;
  - **Lith-MajorOxides**: the eight oxides, 279 classes.

  Each has a "Lith Summary" tab (one central value per class) and one tab
  per class listing every source record and whether the class value is a
  mean or a median.

```{r prefetch, eval = FALSE}
ak_prefetch(x, layers = "rock_chemistry/olson2014")
```

**Audit the class values first.** Rock N needs dedicated analyses and is
rarely part of standard whole-rock geochemistry, so many classes rest on
few records:

```{r audit, eval = FALSE}
lt <- rock_chem_lithologies(c("N", "S", "CaO", "MgO", "P2O5"))
lt |> dplyr::filter(element == "N") |> dplyr::arrange(n)     # records per class, sparse first
lt |> dplyr::filter(element == "N", is.na(tab))              # classes whose records tab wasn't found
```

`n` and `sdlog` come from the per-class tabs. The workbooks' layout is not
documented, so the parser finds columns by their headers. `parse_note` and
`tab` show what it could not match; live test H12 writes the full audit.

## 2. Using it

```{r use, eval = FALSE}
d <- ak_delineate(lat = 63.7255, lon = -148.9670, site_code = "SITE-001")
ak_rock_chem(d)                                  # rock N (default), one catchment

x <- ak_catchments(pts) |>
  ak_rock_chem(element = c("N", "S", "CaO", "MgO", "P2O5"), n = 1000)   # columns appended

# the crosswalk: which SIM 3340 terms matched which class, and the template for modifiers
cw <- rock_chem_crosswalk(x, "N", file = "rock_modifiers.csv")
cw |> dplyr::count(status)                       # ok, sparse class, no matching class, class has no value
# ... fill modifier_class and rationale in rock_modifiers.csv from the Description of Map Units ...
x <- ak_rock_chem(x, "N", modifiers = "rock_modifiers.csv")

# sensitivity checks
ak_rock_chem(x, "N", surficial = "exclude")      # without the mapped surficial deposits
ak_rock_chem(x, "N", formation_sd = 0.5)         # half the record spread as formation-to-formation
ak_rock_chem(x, "N", rank_shares = list(major = c(50, 100), minor = c(10, 50), incidental = c(0, 10),
                                        indeterminate = c(10, 100)))
```

## 3. What you get

For each element `<el>` (`N`, `S`, `CaO`, ...), in percent of rock mass:

- `rock<el>_pct`: the plug-in estimate (class values, rank midpoints), the
  same as Olson and Hawkins's rasters would give;
- `rock<el>_pct_se`, `_lo95`, `_hi95`: from the draws (right-skewed);
- `rock<el>_na_frac`: the share of the mapped area on lithologies without a
  value (not rock types, or no matching class);
- `rock<el>_sparse_frac`: the share of the characterised weight from classes
  with fewer than `min_n` (5) records;
- `rock<el>_coarsened_frac`: the share matched only at a more general term;
- `rock<el>_modifier_frac`: the share whose class was assigned by hand;
- `rock<el>_flag`.

Shared columns: `rock_surficial_frac` (the share in units made only of
unconsolidated deposits) and `rock_mapped_pct`. `details = TRUE` adds the
crosswalk and the map-unit values with their SD.

## 4. Uncertainty: how it is computed

**The match.** Each lithology of a map unit (SIM 3340 table NSALith,
`LITH1` to `LITH5` from general to specific) is matched to an Olson class
by its most specific term. When that term is not a class, the next more
general term is tried and the match counts as coarsened: "Siltstone" not
found becomes "Clastic". Olson and Hawkins added 83 modifier classes for
N and S (78 for the oxides), such as carbonaceous vs. non-carbonaceous
shale, read from formation descriptions. SIM 3340 has no modifier field,
so those are assigned by hand (`modifiers`). For CAKN that means only the
units that intersect the catchments: dozens, not thousands. Log the
rationale for each assignment in the file.

**Prevalence within a unit.** SIM 3340's ranks are defined as shares of
the unit: Major at least 33%, Minor 10-33%, Incidental under 10%.
Indeterminate is taken as 10-100%. The point estimate uses each range's
midpoint, normalised within the unit; the draws pick a share uniformly
within each range and normalise again:

```{r ranks}
ranges <- list(major = c(33, 100), minor = c(10, 33), incidental = c(0, 10))
unit <- c("major", "minor", "minor")                 # e.g. phyllite (major), schist and marble (minor)
mid <- sapply(ranges[unit], mean)
round(mid / sum(mid), 2)                             # point weights
set.seed(1)
w <- t(replicate(5, { s <- sapply(ranges[unit], \(r) runif(1, r[1], r[2])); s / sum(s) }))
round(w, 2)                                          # five draws
```

**Class values.** Rock N within one lithology spans orders of magnitude.
It depends on organic matter, on ammonium substituted for potassium in
micas and feldspars, and on metamorphic grade: devolatilisation removes N,
so a high-grade schist has lost much of what a low-grade one keeps. A
class value is therefore a rough guess for any one formation. Each draw
combines:

- **the class mean**: a shift on the log scale with SD `sdlog/sqrt(n)`
  (how well the class mean is known), shared by every unit of that class;
- **the formation**: a lognormal deviation with SD
  `formation_sd x sdlog`, mean-preserving, for how far this formation's
  rock may sit from its class mean. With `formation_sd = 1` (default),
  all of the spread among records is treated as differences between
  formations. That is conservative: part of it is variation within a
  formation, which averages out over a catchment.

`sdlog` is the SD of the log values among a class's records. A class with
fewer than five records, or with a value but no records found, gets the
90th percentile of `sdlog` among the element's well-sampled classes, so
thin classes carry wide intervals. A map unit draws once per draw, and
every catchment on that unit shares that draw, so errors between
neighbouring catchments are correlated, as they are in reality.

```{r spread}
# what an sdlog of 1 means for a class value of 0.05 % N: the middle 95% of formations
0.05 * exp(-1 / 2 + c(-1.96, 0, 1.96))
```

**Not included:**

- the placement of map boundaries (1:1,584,000; see
  `positional_uncertainty()` and `vignette("geology-sim3340")`);
- lithologies listed wrongly for a unit;
- whether CONUS rocks of a class represent Alaskan rocks of the same name.

That last one is the largest unknown. Live test H12 reports how many Alaska
terms match at all.

## 5. Checking and validating it

- **Vocabulary.** In `rock_chem_crosswalk()`, every `no matching class` row
  is a SIM 3340 term that is not an Olson class name. A few are expected
  (spelling, Alaska-only terms); many would mean the vocabularies differ
  and the match needs a hand-made table. `coarsened` rows show how much
  rests on general terms.
- **Against CONUS.** The CONUS rasters (StreamCat's rock %N) give the
  distribution of map-unit values for similar terrains; Alaska's should
  fall in the same range.
- **Stream chemistry.** Within reference catchments, stream nitrate should
  covary with K and sulfate where rock N is high, if N is released by
  weathering of N-rich sedimentary rocks (ammonium in micas; pyrite in
  carbonaceous shales). Pair this with the oxide exposures, because plain
  lithology differences produce the same co-variation.

## 6. Pitfalls

- **Measurement error attenuates.** A class average for a lithology whose
  rocks vary by orders of magnitude is classical measurement error: a
  regression on `rockN_pct` is biased toward zero, and a null result is weak
  evidence. Model rock N as latent, with `rockN_pct_se` as known error.
- **Concentration is not supply.** Rock N reaches streams only through
  weathering and erosion (Houlton et al. 2018), so the prediction is rock N
  × erosion or runoff, not a main effect. Glacial erosion, permafrost and
  loess cover all modify it in Alaska.
- **Surficial cover.** Till, loess and alluvium of mixed provenance cover
  much of interior Alaska. As mapped, those units get their deposits'
  values (from CONUS deposits of the same name). Report
  `surficial = "exclude"` as the sensitivity, and keep `rock_surficial_frac`
  in the model.
- **Scale.** At 1:1,584,000 a small catchment can sit on a unit that isn't
  there on the ground, and the map can act as an indicator of park or
  region. Compare within regions.
- **Soil N is downstream of rock N.** Adjusting for soil N blocks the
  pathway from rock to stream; for the total effect of rock N, don't.
- **Other rock properties.** Lithology also sets fertility, carbonate
  weathering and permeability. The oxides from the same pipeline (CaO,
  MgO, P2O5) and S are the placebo exposures: rock N should predict stream
  N beyond them.
- `ak_geology()`'s pattern columns (`geol_contains_pct_carbonaceous`,
  `_black_shale`, ...) remain as categorical exposures; keep both for
  comparison.

- Morford, S. L., Houlton, B. Z. and Dahlgren, R. A. (2011). Increased forest ecosystem carbon and nitrogen storage from nitrogen rich bedrock. Nature 477, 78-81.
- Olson, J. R. and Hawkins, C. P. (2012). Predicting natural base-flow stream water chemistry in the western United States. Water Resources Research 48, W02504, doi:10.1029/2011WR011088.
- Olson, J. R. and Hawkins, C. P. (2014). Geochemical characteristics of the conterminous United States. USGS data release, doi:10.5066/F7X0653P.
- Wilson, F. H. et al. (2015). Geologic map of Alaska. USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3340, doi:10.3133/sim3340.
